did_you_know.text: The chapter notes that Samuel had grown old, and as a result he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
Samuel’s sons were named Joel and Abijah, and they served as judges in Beersheba.
Unlike Samuel, his sons did not follow his ways: they pursued dishonest gain, accepted bribes, and perverted justice.
The elders of Israel asked for a king, partly because Samuel had grown old and his sons had not followed his ways; they wanted to be “like all the other nations.”
The LORD explained to Samuel that the people were rejecting not only him, but also the LORD’s reign over them.
The LORD told Samuel to grant the people’s request, but also to warn them and explain to them the “rights of the king” and the cost of having a monarchy.
Samuel warned that the king would draft the people into his army, chariots, and cavalry, and would appoint them to various positions in the government.
One of Samuel’s warnings was that the king might take the best of their fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
The chapter describes the extent of the king’s demands: he would take a tenth of their flocks, and eventually the people might become the king’s slaves.
Despite the warnings, the people insisted on asking for a king to rule over them, lead them, and fight their battles.
